edges.description: Recurrent corneal infection and inflammation injure the corneal nerves.
The corneal infection and inflammation are the keratitis.
The anterior-uveal inflammation is the uveitis.
Trabeculitis raises intraocular pressure, causing secondary glaucoma.
Neurotrophic keratopathy breaks down the corneal epithelium into ulceration.
The necrotizing posterior-segment inflammation is the retinitis.
Retinal necrosis causes severe vision loss.

nodes.description: Intraocular inflammation of the anterior uvea (iritis/uveitis) is frequent in HZO and is accompanied by trabeculitis that raises intraocular pressure and can lead to secondary glaucoma. Uveitis marks eyes at higher risk of other complications and vision loss.

evidence.reference_title: Herpes Zoster Ophthalmicus Uveitis: Onset and Complications.
evidence.snippet: A total of 869 patients with HZO were included for analysis, of whom 413 (47.6%) developed uveitis.

evidence.reference_title: Herpes Zoster Ophthalmicus Uveitis: Onset and Complications.
evidence.snippet: Complications were higher in eyes with uveitis, including moderate or severe vision loss, corneal scarring, neurotrophic keratitis, band keratopathy, corneal melt, elevated intraocular pressure, glaucoma, and cataract

nodes.description: Reactivated virions are carried anterogradely along the ophthalmic nerve to the V1 dermatome (forehead, scalp, upper eyelid), producing the dermatomal vesicular rash and acute neuritis. Involvement of the nasociliary branch (signalled by lesions on the tip of the nose, Hutchinson sign) carries the virus to the ocular surface and interior.

nodes.description: HZO injures the corneal sensory nerves, causing loss of corneal sensation and neurotrophic keratopathy with epithelial breakdown and ulceration. Confocal microscopy shows profound loss of the corneal nerve plexus, even bilaterally in a clinically unilateral disease.

nodes.description: Topical ophthalmic corticosteroids, given alongside antiviral therapy, control the immune-mediated stromal keratitis and anterior uveitis. They must never be used without an antiviral: corticosteroid monotherapy is immunosuppressive and can promote viral replication and precipitate acute retinal necrosis.
